text: California's AB 1228 was signed on September 28, 2023 and set a $20 hourly minimum wage for covered fast-food restaurant employees effective April 1, 2024.

AB 1228 covers limited-service restaurants (customers order and pay before eating) that belong to a chain of at least 60 establishments nationwide and earn more than half their revenue from food and beverages for immediate consumption, including franchisees and coffee, ice-cream and donut shops; it exempts on-site bread bakeries, restaurants inside large grocery stores staffed by the grocer, and restaurants in airports, hotels, large event centres, theme parks, museums, gambling establishments and certain concession locations.

California's general minimum wage orders for 2025 and 2026 state no fast-food dollar rate; they name fast-food restaurant employers under Labor Code section 1474 as subject to a separate minimum 'effective April 1, 2024' and refer to supplements, while the general minimum rose from $16.00 (2024) to $16.50 (2025) and $16.90 (2026). The Labor Commissioner's Minimum Wage page (dated December 2025) states that covered fast-food employees must be paid at least $20.00 per hour starting April 1, 2024 and lists no later fast-food rate, and the Economic Policy Institute reported on March 23, 2026 that the Fast Food Council had not yet taken up a cost-of-living adjustment because its chair resigned in June 2025 and no new chair had been named.
The Fast Food Council may raise the fast-food minimum wage annually by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the change in the CPI, with no increase before January 1, 2025.

Using monthly QCEW data through December 2024, Clemens, Edwards and Meer (2025) estimate that California fast-food employment fell 2.7 percent relative to the rest of the United States between September 2023 and September 2024, 3.2 percent after removing pre-enactment trends, with eight DD and DDD estimates ranging from -2.28 to -3.93 percent (Table 1) and placebo-based rather than standard-error-based inference.

In the revised version (October 2026), Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen extend the QCEW analysis to September 2025 and add QWI data; their eight two-year QCEW estimates range from -2.02 to -5.03 percent with a median of -3.45 percent (Table 3), and the two-year QWI median is -3.52 percent (Table 7).

Dube (2026), using quarterly QCEW data through 2025Q3 and 20 federal-minimum-wage control states, estimates a fast-food wage effect of about 7 to 7.5 percent and an employment effect of -1.39 percent (Ferman-Pinto SE 0.44) by event-study difference-in-differences and -0.26 percent (SE 0.54) by synthetic difference-in-differences, his preferred estimate, measured as the 2024Q2-2025Q3 average relative to 2023Q4 (Table 1, Panel A).

Dube (2026, Table D1) attributes most of the gap between Clemens et al.'s and his QCEW estimates to detrending, population normalization, multi-quarter pre- and post-period averaging windows (one step that replaces Clemens et al.'s September 2023 base with the 2022Q1-2023Q3 average and their single post month with the 2024Q2-2025Q3 average) and synthetic-control weighting, and finds seasonal adjustment and the choice of control states nearly irrelevant.

Sosinskiy and Reich (2026), using county-level QCEW data for 2022-2024 with 2024Q1 as reference period and a triple difference against full-service restaurants, estimate an employment-rate effect of -0.9 percent in 2024Q4 with a Rambachan-Roth 95 percent interval of -2.9 to 0.9 percent (Table 1).

Across 1,440 synthetic-control and synthetic DID specifications using QCEW and QWI data through 2025Q4, Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen (2026) find that over 96 percent of estimated employment effects are negative, that the median QCEW SDID estimate is -3.58 percent, and that Dube's SDID estimate lies near the 97th percentile.

With establishment-level YTS data through 2025, Melo, Neumark, Sigaud and Wagner (2026) find a small, insignificant state-level employment effect (IHS coefficient -0.0137, placebo SE 0.0240; Table 2, Panel A, column 2) but significant chain-by-state declines among smaller chains (IHS coefficients about -0.23; Table 3), and no significant effect for the 20 largest chains.

Using Equifax payroll data for large fast-food employers from July 2023 to January 2025, Hamdi and Sovich (2025) find hourly wages rose 12.1 percent and establishment employment changed by +2.3 percent (95 percent CI -1.0 to 5.5), as lower hiring was outweighed by lower turnover.

No causal or pre-specified estimate of AB 1228's employment effect found uses QCEW data for any 2026 quarter; the latest causal estimates use QCEW data through 2025Q4 (Clemens et al. 2026, synthetic controls) or 2025Q3 (Dube 2026; Clemens et al. 2026 revision). A descriptive comparison that is not a causal estimate is public: Steier (2026) indexes California and rest-of-US NAICS 722513 employment to September 2023 through March 2026 (2026Q1 release).
The BLS released preliminary QCEW data for the first quarter of 2026 on August 28, 2026; second-quarter 2026 data are scheduled for December 2, 2026.

QCEW monthly employment counts covered workers who worked or received pay in the pay period including the 12th of the month, counting multiple job holders once per employer; the average weekly wage is total quarterly wages divided by mean monthly employment and by 13.

About 60 percent of the most detailed QCEW cells are suppressed for confidentiality (marked by disclosure code N in the open-data files), but published higher-level totals include the suppressed data; preliminary data are finalized with the next year's first-quarter release.

QCEW open-data CSV slices by industry or area cover the most recent five years at data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/{year}/{qtr}/industry/{naics}.csv; county by six-digit NAICS by ownership cells have aggregation level 78 and private ownership code 5.

NAICS 722513 (Limited-Service Restaurants) covers establishments where patrons order or select items and pay before eating, excluding snack and nonalcoholic beverage bars (722515, e.g. coffee and donut shops); 722511 (Full-Service Restaurants) covers establishments where patrons are served while seated and pay after eating.

Sosinskiy and Reich (2026) estimate that about 70 percent of the workers in California's fast-food restaurants and snack and nonalcoholic beverage bars combined (NAICS 722513 and 722515) are covered by the $20 minimum wage; they give no coverage share for NAICS 722513 alone.

Clemens et al. measure effects from the September 2023 enactment and argue firms responded in anticipation, while Sosinskiy and Reich use the quarter before implementation as reference and find no anticipation effect, and Dube uses 2023Q4 as base and drops 2024Q1 as a transition quarter.

Dube (2026) reports every Table 1 estimate under a second base, the 2022Q1-2023Q3 pre-period average, which he describes as invariant to anticipation in 2023Q4 (2024Q1 is excluded as a transition quarter in both versions); with that base the QCEW fast-food employment effect moves from -1.39 to -1.28 percent (DD) and from -0.26 to -0.02 percent (SDID) (Table 1, Panels A and B; p. 6).

Re-estimating with Clemens et al.'s September 2023 reference period, Sosinskiy and Reich (2026, Table A3) estimate fast-food employment-rate effects of -0.2 percent in 2023Q4 (95 percent CI -1.9 to 1.7) and -0.6 percent in 2024Q1 (-4.5 to 2.7) in their preferred county-level specification, and -0.5 and -1.4 percent in the specification closest to Clemens et al.; they conclude there is no anticipation effect and that almost 60 percent of Clemens et al.'s estimated effect occurs between enactment and implementation (pp. 42-43).

Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen (2026, w35931) fit their synthetic controls with Dube's 2023Q4 base and 2024Q1 transition quarter, measure their fixed-horizon estimates from 2023Q3, and report that the distribution of estimates is slightly more negative but not meaningfully changed with a 2023Q3 baseline and no transition quarter (footnote 5).

Re-estimated on Dube's 2023Q4 base, Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen's one-year QWI estimates range from -0.59 to -2.47 percent with a median of -1.43 percent, against a median of -1.38 percent on their 2023Q3 base, and none is significant at the 10 percent level (w34033 revision, footnote 9 and Tables A3-A4).

AB 1228 replaced AB 257, the FAST Recovery Act, signed in September 2022 (September 5, 2022), which would have let a Fast Food Council set a minimum wage of up to $22 per hour in 2023 for fast-food chains with 100 or more locations nationwide, with annual increases of up to the lesser of 3.5 percent or inflation. Opponents' referendum petition (signatures submitted in December 2022) led a Sacramento court to block the law in December 2022 and January 2023 and qualified for the November 2024 ballot on January 24, 2023, which froze the law before it took effect; the September 2023 compromise enacted AB 1228 instead, and the referendum was withdrawn on December 29, 2023. No source reports a wage set under AB 257.

In Louisiana QCEW microdata matched by name to fast-food chains, Melo, Neumark, Sigaud and Wagner (2026) find that only 77.7 percent of chain restaurant locations are coded NAICS 722513, 9.2 percent 722515, 7.9 percent full-service 722511 and 0.7 percent 722514 or 722320, and that 17 of 121 chains (14 percent) have locations in both 722513 and another restaurant code; they warn that the bias from such misclassification can be more complex than attenuation if classification patterns change with the composition changes a higher minimum wage causes (pp. 15-16 and footnote 20).

Melo et al. (2026) report that in 2025 employment at California establishments matched by exact name to limited-service chains with at least 60 locations (YTS data) is 33 percent smaller than QCEW NAICS 722513 employment (the YTS-QCEW gap ranges from 49 percent below QCEW in the District of Columbia to 4 percent above it in Iowa), and that the 2019-2025 percentage change in QCEW 722513 employment minus the YTS change ranges from -8 points (Alabama) to +17 points (District of Columbia), which they note can bias difference-in-differences designs (p. 19, Figures 4-5).

Ferman and Pinto (2019) show that variation in group sizes makes the aggregate DID model heteroskedastic, so that inference methods assuming homoskedasticity misstate the size of tests with few treated groups, and derive a residual-bootstrap test with a heteroskedasticity correction that is valid with one treated group as the number of control groups grows, under the assumptions that the treated group's errors share the control groups' distribution conditional on covariates such as group size and differ across groups only by a scale parameter; in their simulations it performs reasonably with 25 groups, with a minor size distortion when the treated group is among the smallest.

Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) note that their jackknife variance estimator is not defined with one treated unit and propose a placebo variance estimator that reassigns treatment to control units; its validity relies on homoskedasticity across units, which they describe as effectively necessary for inference with one treated unit.

Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) introduce synthetic control placebo inference that applies the method to every control unit and compares the treated unit's post/pre mean squared prediction error ratio with the placebo distribution (California ranks first of 39 units, p = 1/39 = 0.026, in their application), suggest in-time placebos when comparison units are few, and note that with anticipation the intervention date should be moved to the first period in which outcomes may react.

Abadie (2021) advises that synthetic control weights can be computed, and preregistered, without post-treatment outcomes as a safeguard against specification searches, that effects similar in size to the outcome's volatility are hard to detect, that the intervention should be backdated to before any anticipation, and that backdating gives an in-time placebo test of the estimator's credibility (pp. 406, 409-410, 414).

Chernozhukov, Wuthrich and Zhu (2021) propose permutation (conformal) inference for synthetic control and related counterfactual estimators that permutes residuals over time; it is approximately valid when the errors are stationary and weakly dependent and the counterfactual estimator is consistent or stable, exact under exchangeability, with finite-sample bounds that become exact as the number of pre-treatment periods grows.

Ferman, Pinto and Possebom (2020) find substantial room for specification searching across commonly used synthetic control specifications when the number of pre-treatment periods is finite (with 12 pre-periods and seven specifications, a 5 percent test rejects in at least one specification with probability about 14 percent), even when the choice is restricted to specifications with a good pre-treatment fit, and recommend reporting results for several specifications.

Conley and Taber (2011) develop inference for DID with a small number of policy changes by using the residuals of the many control groups to estimate the distribution of the treatment effect estimator, assuming the errors are independent and identically distributed across groups and independent of treatment.

The two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure declares equivalence within prespecified bounds when both one-sided tests reject at level alpha, which is the same as the 1 - 2 alpha (for alpha = 0.05, 90 percent) confidence interval lying inside the bounds (Schuirmann 1987; Lakens 2017).

A public descriptive series (Steier 2026) using QCEW NAICS 722513 monthly employment through the first quarter of 2026 puts California at 97.06 and the rest of the United States at 98.99 in March 2026 (September 2023 = 100), with California 1.65 percent and the rest of the United States 0.90 percent below their March 2024 levels; it makes no causal estimate.

Card and Krueger (1994), surveying 410 fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania before and after New Jersey's 1992 minimum wage increase from $4.25 to $5.05, find no indication that the increase reduced employment.

Using county-level QCEW data on private NAICS 722513 for 36 populous California and New York counties and a stacked synthetic control estimator with donor counties in federal-minimum-wage states, Wiltshire, McPherson, Reich and Sosinskiy (2026) find substantial pay growth and no disemployment during the run-up of minimum wages to $15, and positive employment effects after 2020.

Clemens, Edwards, Meer and Nguyen (2026, w34990) estimate that food-away-from-home prices in California's four CPI metropolitan areas rose 3.3 to 3.6 percent relative to 17 control areas through December 2024, that prices began rising in the months between AB 1228's enactment and implementation, and that the increase likely arises in part from spillovers to full-service restaurants.

In the first version of their study (September 2024), Reich and Sosinskiy estimate from Glassdoor job posts that AB 1228 raised average hourly pay of fast-food workers by 18 percent without reducing employment, and from scraped menus that prices rose about 3.7 percent.

Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (2019), comparing excess jobs at or just above new minimum wages with missing jobs below them across 138 state minimum wage increases from 1979 to 2016, find the number of low-wage jobs essentially unchanged over the five years after an increase.

Dube, Reich, Bhatt and Sosinskiy (2024, revised 2026) argue that disemployment estimates for restaurants from multi-state commuting zones are confounded by 1990s pre-trend violations amplified by two-way fixed effects, and that modern event-study designs show no meaningful restaurant employment decline.

Neumark and Rodriguez-Lopez (2026) re-estimate the stacked and local-projection event-study designs of the recent minimum wage literature on the same data, find negative and significant employment effects, more strongly in restaurants, and argue that the null results depend on choices of variables, events, sample definitions and weighting.

Thornberg (2025) reports that California's March 2025 benchmark revision of its CES payroll estimates, which aligns them with QCEW data, lowered December 2024 limited-service restaurant employment by 21,500 jobs (2.5 percent) and turned a roughly flat 2024 into a 3.2 percent decline over the 12 months to January 2025.

For California's Proposition 99 (39 states, 1970-2000, treated from 1989, 19 pre- and 12 post-treatment years), Arkhangelsky et al. (2021, Table 1) report estimates of the effect on per-capita cigarette sales of -15.6 (placebo standard error 8.4) for synthetic difference-in-differences, -19.6 (9.9) for synthetic control and -27.3 (17.7) for difference-in-differences.

Synthetic difference-in-differences (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021, Algorithm 1) chooses simplex unit weights with an intercept and a ridge penalty zeta^2 Tpre ||omega||^2, where zeta = (Ntr Tpost)^(1/4) times the standard deviation of control units' pre-period first differences, chooses simplex time weights with an intercept and a negligible penalty, and estimates the effect by a doubly weighted two-way fixed effects regression; their synthetic control comparison omits the intercept and the time weights.

Demeaning outcomes by their pre-treatment averages before fitting synthetic control weights is equivalent to relaxing the synthetic control no-intercept restriction, as Doudchenko and Imbens (2016) propose; Ferman and Pinto (2021) show that with imperfect pre-treatment fit the original estimator is generally biased even as the pre-period grows, while the demeaned version is asymptotically unbiased under conditions under which DID is, and has lower asymptotic mean squared error than DID under an additional stability assumption.

State resident population on July 1 comes from the Census Bureau's Population Estimates Program: the 2010-2020 intercensal estimates (released September 2025) for 2010-2019 and the Vintage 2025 estimates (released January 2026) for 2020-2025.

The Proposition 99 panel used to check the estimator code is the california_prop99 file distributed with the synthdid R package, a long-format version of the Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) data on per-capita cigarette sales for 39 states, 1970-2000.

In each of the 20 D20 states (Alabama, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Wisconsin, Wyoming) the binding minimum wage for employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act was the federal $7.25 on 1 January of every year from 2014 to 2020, so throughout 2014-2019: Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Tennessee had no state minimum wage law; Georgia and Wyoming had state rates of $5.15, below the federal rate; Oklahoma's rate was $7.25 for larger employers and $2.00 for small ones; and the other twelve had a state rate of exactly $7.25 in every year.

Of the 30 comparison units outside California and D20, 27 states and the District of Columbia changed their state minimum wage between 1 January 2014 and 1 January 2019 (Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia, District of Columbia); Virginia stayed at $7.25 through 1 January 2020, and Nevada's rate (7.25-8.25) is unchanged from 2014 to 2019 in the Labor Department's January 1 series and changes only in its 2020 column.
